claim: Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne illness in the United States, affecting an estimated 500,000 people each year.
source: Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne illness in the United States, affecting an estimated 500,000 people each year (Kugeler et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kugeler et al., 2021

claim: The spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative agent of Lyme disease.
source: The spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative agent of Lyme disease and is primarily transmitted by Ixodes scapularis ticks in North America (Mead, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mead, 2022

claim: Borrelia burgdorferi is primarily transmitted by Ixodes scapularis ticks in North America.
source: The spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative agent of Lyme disease and is primarily transmitted by Ixodes scapularis ticks in North America (Mead, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mead, 2022

claim: Between 2008 and 2015, arthritis was the major manifestation in a third of Lyme disease cases reported to the CDC.
source: However, between 2008 and 2015, arthritis was the major manifestation in a third of Lyme disease cases reported to the CDC (Arvikar and Steere, 2022; Schwartz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arvikar and Steere, 2022 and Schwartz et al., 2017

claim: A small percentage of Lyme arthritis patients experience persistent joint inflammation for months or several years, termed post-infectious Lyme arthritis.
source: Although Lyme arthritis resolves completely with antibiotic therapy in most patients, a small percentage of individuals experience persistent joint inflammation for months or several years, termed post-infectious Lyme arthritis (Arvikar and Steere, 2022; Steere et al., 1987; Lochhead et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arvikar and Steere, 2022; Steere et al., 1987; Lochhead et al., 2021

claim: Synovial fluid from Lyme arthritis patients contains infiltrating polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs), IFN-γ-producing mononuclear cells, and large amounts of NF-κB-induced pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
source: Studies of synovial fluid from Lyme arthritis patients found infiltrating polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs), IFN-γ-producing mononuclear cells, and large amounts of NF-κB-induced pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, such as IL-6, CXCL10, and TNF-α (Miller and Aucott, 2021; Shin et al., 2007; Lochhead et al., 2019b; Gross et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miller and Aucott, 2021; Shin et al., 2007; Lochhead et al., 2019b; Gross et al., 1998

claim: An inverse correlation exists between the robust IFN-γ signature and tissue repair in synovial tissue and fluid from patients with post-infectious Lyme arthritis.
source: An inverse correlation between the robust IFN-γ signature and tissue repair has been demonstrated in the synovial tissue and fluid from patients with post-infectious Lyme arthritis (Lochhead et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lochhead et al., 2019a

claim: B. burgdorferi infection of laboratory mice causes an acute arthritis, the severity of which is mouse strain dependent.
source: B. burgdorferi infection of laboratory mice causes an acute arthritis, the severity of which is mouse strain dependent (Barthold et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barthold et al., 1990

claim: B. burgdorferi-infected C3H/HeN mice develop pronounced neutrophilic infiltration of periarticular structures and the synovial lining, which peaks in severity several weeks after infection.
source: B. burgdorferi-infected-C3H/HeN mice develop pronounced neutrophilic infiltration of periarticular structures and the synovial lining, which peaks in severity several weeks after infection (Barthold et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barthold et al., 1993

claim: Infection of B. burgdorferi C57BL/6 mice causes mild, if any, arthritis.
source: In contrast, infection of B. burgdorferi C57BL/6 mice causes mild, if any, arthritis (Ma et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 1998

claim: Rag1-/- and SCID mice on a C57BL/6 background are resistant to B. burgdorferi-induced arthritis.
source: On a C57BL/6 background, the immune-deficient Rag1-/- and SCID mice are also resistant to B. burgdorferi-induced arthritis, indicating that responses independent of humoral and cellular immunity contribute to the milder phenotype of disease in these animals (Brown and Reiner, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown and Reiner, 1999

claim: Neutrophils, macrophages, and signaling involving IFN-γ and NF-κB contribute to the severity of murine joint inflammation.
source: Similar to Lyme arthritis in humans, neutrophils, macrophages, and signaling involving IFN-γ and NF-κB contribute to the severity of murine joint inflammation (Ritzman et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2003; Anguita et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ritzman et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2003; Anguita et al., 2002

claim: SLPI is a 12 kDa, secreted, non-glycosylated, cysteine-rich protein.
source: The secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor (SLPI) is a 12 kDa, secreted, non-glycosylated, cysteine-rich protein (Doumas et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doumas et al., 2005

claim: SLPI strongly inhibits serine proteases, especially neutrophil-derived serine proteases including cathepsin G and elastase.
source: It strongly inhibits serine proteases, especially neutrophil-derived serine proteases (NSPs), including cathepsin G (CTSG) and elastase (NE) (Thompson and Ohlsson, 1986; Moreau et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thompson and Ohlsson, 1986; Moreau et al., 2008

claim: SLPI is secreted by epithelial cells at various mucosal surfaces and is also produced by neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells, and fibroblasts.
source: It is secreted by epithelial cells at various mucosal surfaces and is also produced by neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells, and fibroblasts (Maruyama et al., 1994; Sallenave et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maruyama et al., 1994; Sallenave et al., 1994

claim: The major function of SLPI is to inhibit excessive protease activity at sites of inflammation, thus promoting tissue repair and wound healing.
source: The major function of SLPI is to inhibit excessive protease activity at sites of inflammation, thus promoting tissue repair and wound healing (Ashcroft et al., 2000; Zhu et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ashcroft et al., 2000; Zhu et al., 2002

claim: SLPI exerts anti-inflammatory function by inhibiting NF-κB activation in macrophages.
source: SLPI also exerts anti-inflammatory function by inhibiting NF-κB activation in macrophages (Taggart et al., 2005; Taggart et al., 2002; Jin et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taggart et al., 2005; Taggart et al., 2002; Jin et al., 1997

claim: Neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G induce potent destruction of cartilage proteoglycan in vitro and in vivo, contributing to rheumatoid arthritis progression.
source: NE and CTSG induce potent destruction of cartilage proteoglycan in vitro and in vivo, which contributes to rheumatoid arthritis progression (McDonnell et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to McDonnell et al., 1993

claim: SLPI inhibits joint inflammation and bone destruction.
source: Some studies also demonstrated that SLPI inhibits joint inflammation and bone destruction (Lee et al., 2016; Song et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2016; Song et al., 1999

claim: Slpi-deficient C57BL/6 mice infected with B. burgdorferi had a significantly higher infection burden in the tibiotarsal joints compared to infected wild-type control mice.
source: Strikingly, we observed a significantly higher spirochete burden in the ankle joints of infected Slpi-/- mice (n=24) between 21 and 24 dpi (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: No significant difference in infection burden was observed in the skin between WT and Slpi-/- mice at 7, 14, or 21-24 days post-infection.
source: We did not observe any significant difference in infection burden in the skin between WT and Slpi-/- mice (n=24) at 7, 14, 21–24 dpi, or in the heart between 21–24 dpi (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-D

claim: No significant difference in infection burden was observed in the heart between WT and Slpi-/- mice at 21-24 days post-infection.
source: We did not observe any significant difference in infection burden in the skin between WT and Slpi-/- mice (n=24) at 7, 14, 21–24 dpi, or in the heart between 21–24 dpi (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-D

claim: Significant swelling was observed solely in the infected Slpi-/- mice at around 24 days post-infection.
source: Furthermore, at around 24 dpi, significant swelling was also observed solely in the infected Slpi-/- mice (Figure 2A, red arrow).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 14 out of 20 infected Slpi-/- mice displayed visible swelling (score ≥1), while only 1 in 14 infected WT mice displayed mild swelling (score 1) at the ankle.
source: While 14 out of 20 infected Slpi-/- mice displayed visible swelling (score ≥1), only 1 in 14 infected WT mice displayed mild swelling (score 1) at the ankle (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Inflammation of bursa and soft tissue adjacent to the tibiotarsal joint was consistently observed in the infected Slpi-/- mice.
source: Inflammation of bursa and soft tissue adjacent to the tibiotarsal joint, but not in the tibiotarsal synovium, was consistently observed in the infected Slpi-/- mice (Figure 2C, black rectangle).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Only 1 out of 14 infected WT mice displayed modest inflammation (score = 2) in the bursa and soft tissue adjacent to the tibiotarsal joint.
source: In contrast, only 1 out of 14 infected WT mice displayed modest inflammation (score = 2) in these sites (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Significantly higher percentages of infiltrating neutrophils were observed in the ankle joints of infected Slpi-/- mice compared to WT mice.
source: After gating, we observed significantly higher percentages of infiltrating neutrophils and macrophages in the dissected tissues from infected Slpi-/- than WT mice (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Significantly higher percentages of infiltrating macrophages were observed in the ankle joints of infected Slpi-/- mice compared to WT mice.
source: After gating, we observed significantly higher percentages of infiltrating neutrophils and macrophages in the dissected tissues from infected Slpi-/- than WT mice (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Increased gene expression of Cxcr2 was detected in the tibiotarsal tissues of B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-deficient mice.
source: Using RT-qPCR on the tibiotarsal tissues extracted from B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-/- mice, we detected increased gene expression of neutrophil chemoattractant receptor C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (Cxcr2), monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (Mcp-1), and its receptor C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (Ccr2) (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Increased gene expression of Mcp-1 was detected in the tibiotarsal tissues of B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-deficient mice.
source: Using RT-qPCR on the tibiotarsal tissues extracted from B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-/- mice, we detected increased gene expression of neutrophil chemoattractant receptor C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (Cxcr2), monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (Mcp-1), and its receptor C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (Ccr2) (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Increased gene expression of Ccr2 was detected in the tibiotarsal tissues of B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-deficient mice.
source: Using RT-qPCR on the tibiotarsal tissues extracted from B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-/- mice, we detected increased gene expression of neutrophil chemoattractant receptor C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (Cxcr2), monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (Mcp-1), and its receptor C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (Ccr2) (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: A significant increase in IL-6 was observed in infected Slpi-/- mice.
source: We observed a significant increase in IL-6 in infected Slpi-/- mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: A significantly higher level of neutrophil elastase was observed solely in the serum of infected Slpi-/- mice.
source: Indeed, using ELISA, we observed a significantly higher level of NE solely in the serum of infected Slpi-/- mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: An increased serum level of neutrophil elastase was observed in B. burgdorferi-infected, arthritis-susceptible C3H/HeN mice at 21 days post-infection.
source: An increased serum level of NE was also observed in the B. burgdorferi-infected, arthritis-susceptible C3H/HeN mice at 21 dpi (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H

claim: A significant increase in the levels of MMP-8 was observed solely in the infected Slpi-/- mice.
source: We observed a significant increase in the levels of MMP-8 solely in the infected Slpi-/- mice (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I

claim: The serum level of SLPI showed a significant decrease in Lyme disease patients compared to healthy adult controls.
source: The serum level of human SLPI assessed by ELISA showed a significant decrease in the SLPI level in Lyme disease patients comparing to healthy adult controls (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Human SLPI passed the significance threshold in BASEHIT screening, indicating B. burgdorferi-SLPI binding.
source: Human SLPI is one of the exoproteins that passed the significance threshold, indicating B. burgdorferi-SLPI binding.
evidence: Supported by BASEHIT screening data

claim: Strong binding was observed between whole-cell B. burgdorferi lysates and human SLPI at a level as low as 10 nM.
source: We observed strong binding between whole-cell B. burgdorferi lysates and hSLPI at a level as low as 10 nM (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: A significant increase in fluorescence intensity was observed when B. burgdorferi, cultivated at 33°C, was incubated with human SLPI at 10 nM and 1 µM level.
source: A significant increase in fluorescence intensity was observed when B. burgdorferi, cultivated at 33°C, was incubated with human SLPI at 10 nM and 1 µM level (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: A significant increase in fluorescence intensity was observed when B. burgdorferi were incubated with 1 µM recombinant murine SLPI.
source: Though the binding to 10 nM rmSLPI was at background level, we observed a significant increase in fluorescence intensity when B. burgdorferi were incubated with 1 µM rmSLPI (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Flow cytometry demonstrated increased binding of B. burgdorferi cultured at 37°C to 1 µM human SLPI or recombinant murine SLPI.
source: Flow cytometry also demonstrated increased binding of B. burgdorferi cultured at 37°C to 1 µM hSLPI or rmSLPI (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C

claim: No binding was observed between human SLPI and B. burgdorferi B31A, a high-passage non-infectious strain.
source: In contrast to B. burgdorferi B31-A3, an infectious strain used throughout this study, we did not observe any binding between hSLPI and B. burgdorferi B31A, a high-passage non-infectious strain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Caine and Coburn, 2015; Elias et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and citations to Caine and Coburn, 2015; Elias et al., 2002

claim: After treatment with proteinase K, a marked decrease in binding of human SLPI to B. burgdorferi lysates was observed.
source: After treatment with proteinase K, we observed a marked decrease in binding of hSLPI to B. burgdorferi lysates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: No significant changes in B. burgdorferi viability were observed in the presence of human SLPI.
source: However, using the BacTiter-Glow microbial cell viability assay, we did not observe any significant changes in B. burgdorferi viability in the presence of hSLPI (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: Pre-incubation of human SLPI did not protect spirochetes from killing by mouse B. burgdorferi antisera.
source: However, again, using the BacTiter-Glow microbial cell viability assay, the pre-incubation of hSLPI did not protect spirochetes from killing by mouse B. burgdorferi antisera (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: SLPI is important in suppressing periarticular joint inflammation in Lyme disease.
source: These data demonstrate the importance of SLPI in suppressing periarticular joint inflammation in Lyme disease.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data presented in the study

claim: SLPI directly interacts with B. burgdorferi.
source: Moreover, using a recently developed BASEHIT (BActerial Selection to Elucidate Host-microbe Interactions in high Throughput) library, we found that SLPI directly interacts with B. burgdorferi.
evidence: Supported by BASEHIT screening and subsequent validation experiments

claim: The dysregulated excessive pro-inflammatory responses inhibit tissue repair and lead to extensive tissue damage in Lyme arthritis.
source: This suggests that the dysregulated excessive pro-inflammatory responses inhibit tissue repair and lead to extensive tissue damage.
evidence: Inference based on cited studies of synovial tissue and fluid from patients with post-infectious Lyme arthritis

claim: IL-6 recruits and stimulates neutrophils, leading to the secretion of neutrophil-derived serine proteases including neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G.
source: IL-6 recruits and stimulates neutrophils, leading to the secretion of neutrophil-derived serine proteases including neutrophil elastase (NE) and cathepsin G (CTSG) (Srirangan and Choy, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Srirangan and Choy, 2010

claim: The lack of serine protease inhibitors, such as SLPI, can cause excessive protease activity and subsequent tissue damage and inflammation.
source: The lack of serine protease inhibitors, such as SLPI, can cause excessive protease activity and subsequent tissue damage and inflammation (Wilkinson et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilkinson et al., 2019

claim: A correlation exists between IL-6, macrophages, metalloproteinases (MMPs), and articular cartilage destruction in the synovial tissue of rheumatoid arthritis patients.
source: A correlation between IL-6, macrophages, metalloproteinases (MMPs), and articular cartilage destruction has been observed in the synovial tissue of RA patients (Murphy and Nagase, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murphy and Nagase, 2008

claim: Elevated levels of host matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) have been found in the synovial fluid of Lyme arthritis patients and can cause excessive tissue damage.
source: Elevated levels of host matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) have also been found in the synovial fluid of Lyme arthritis patients and can cause excessive tissue damage (Hu et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2001

claim: The significant increase in the infection burden in Slpi-/- mice can contribute to the enhanced periarticular inflammation following B. burgdorferi infection.
source: The significant increase in the infection burden in Slpi-/- mice can contribute to the enhanced periarticular inflammation following B. burgdorferi infection.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing higher infection burden in Slpi-/- mice

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of SLPI significantly decreased the severity of joint swelling in a Streptococcal cell wall (SCW)-induced arthritis model in rats.
source: Indeed, in a Streptococcal cell wall (SCW)-induced arthritis model in rats, the intraperitoneal injection of SLPI significantly decreased the severity of joint swelling (Song et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 1999

claim: A high percentage of neutrophils is present in the synovial fluid during active B. burgdorferi infection.
source: This observation is consistent with clinical studies that showed a high percentage of neutrophils in the synovial fluid during active infection (Lochhead et al., 2017; Grillon et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lochhead et al., 2017; Grillon et al., 2019

claim: In post-infectious Lyme arthritis, fewer neutrophils and more macrophages are present in patients' synovial fluid.
source: In post-infectious Lyme arthritis, fewer neutrophils and more macrophages are present in patients' synovial fluid (Lochhead et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lochhead et al., 2021

claim: The neutrophil chemoattractant KC (CXCL1) and receptor CXCR2 mediate neutrophil recruitment and are critical for the development of murine Lyme arthritis.
source: The neutrophil chemoattractant KC (CXCL1) and receptor CXCR2 mediates neutrophil recruitment and is critical for the development of murine Lyme arthritis.
evidence: Supported by subsequent statement about Kc-/- and Cxcr2-/- mice

claim: Both Kc-/- and Cxcr2-/- C3H mice developed significantly less ankle swelling when infected with B. burgdorferi.
source: Both Kc-/- and Cxcr2-/- C3H mice developed significantly less ankle swelling when infected with B. burgdorferi (Ritzman et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ritzman et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2003

claim: Monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1/CCL2) and receptor CCR2 contribute to macrophage infiltration.
source: Monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1/CCL2) and receptor CCR2 contribute to macrophage infiltration (Deshmane et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deshmane et al., 2009

claim: A high level of MCP-1 was detected in the tibiotarsal tissues of B. burgdorferi-infected, arthritis-susceptible C3H/He mice.
source: Though little to no difference in arthritis was observed in the Ccr2-/- mice, a high level of MCP-1 was detected in the tibiotarsal tissues of B. burgdorferi-infected, arthritis-susceptible C3H/He mice, suggesting a function for macrophages (Brown et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2003

claim: An elevated IL-6 level has been demonstrated in the serum, synovial fluid, and synovial tissue from Lyme arthritis patients.
source: An elevated IL-6 level has been demonstrated in the serum, synovial fluid, and synovial tissue from Lyme arthritis patients (Lochhead et al., 2019b; Lochhead et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lochhead et al., 2019b; Lochhead et al., 2017

claim: IL-6 is pivotal in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis and correlates with the disease severity and joint destruction.
source: IL-6 is also pivotal in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis and correlates with the disease severity and joint destruction (Srirangan and Choy, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Srirangan and Choy, 2010

claim: IL-6 recruited neutrophils in an in vitro co-culture rheumatoid arthritis model.
source: It has been shown that IL-6 recruited neutrophils in an in vitro co-culture rheumatoid arthritis model (Lally et al., 2005).

claim: Neutrophils can be activated by IL-6 through binding of IL-6 receptor (IL-6R).
source: Neutrophils can be activated by IL-6 through binding of IL-6 receptor (IL-6R) (Srirangan and Choy, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Srirangan and Choy, 2010

claim: Activated neutrophils release several neutrophil serine proteases including neutrophil elastase (NE), cathepsin G (CTSG), and proteinase-3 (PR3), which can lead to potent cartilage destruction.
source: Activated neutrophils release several NSPs including neutrophil elastase (NE), cathepsin G (CTSG), and proteinase-3 (PR3), which can lead to potent cartilage destruction (Wilkinson et al., 2019).

claim: No significant changes in TNF-α serum protein levels were observed in B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-/- and WT mice.
source: Interestingly, despite the known function of TNF-α in inflammatory responses, we did not observe any significant changes in either TNF-α serum protein levels or Tnf-α gene expression levels in the B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-/- and WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: No significant changes in Tnf-α gene expression levels were observed in B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-/- and WT mice.
source: Interestingly, despite the known function of TNF-α in inflammatory responses, we did not observe any significant changes in either TNF-α serum protein levels or Tnf-α gene expression levels in the B. burgdorferi-infected Slpi-/- and WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Previous microarray data did not show significant changes in TNF-α levels in C57BL/6 mice following B. burgdorferi infection.
source: The result is consistent with previous microarray data that did not show significant changes in TNF-α levels in the C57BL/6 mice following B. burgdorferi infection (Crandall et al., 2006).

claim: MMPs target extracellular matrix and cause articular cartilage destruction.

claim: MMP-8 is known as neutrophil collagenase.
source: MMP-8 is known as neutrophil collagenase (Wen et al., 2015).

claim: The level of MMP-8 was significantly higher in patients with post-infectious Lyme arthritis than patients with active infection.

claim: Elevated levels of MMP-1, -3, -13, and -19 were revealed in the synovial fluid of Lyme arthritis patients.

claim: The median level of SLPI in healthy subjects tested in this study (38.92 ng/ml) is comparable with previous studies showing on average about 40 ng/ml SLPI in the serum from healthy volunteers.

claim: B. burgdorferi interacts with various mammalian proteins, including decorin, fibronectin, and plasminogen.
